newsitem.title: USA: UK security regulator calls for global cooperation.
newsitem.headline: UK security regulator calls for global cooperation.

text.p: As capital markets become increasingly global, regulators from different countries must work together to mitigate the possibility of a worldwide financial calamity, Britian's top securities regulator said Thursday.

"Recent events, such as Barings and Sumitomo, have all shown that we are increasingly -- from a supervisory point of view -- interdependent," Securities and Investments Board Chairman Sir Andrew Large.
Therefore, regulators will "focus increasingly on the need to mitigate systemic risk," Large said in a speech at an American Bar Association study group here.
"We have a shared stewardship for the integrity of our global financial markets," Large told the audience of U.S. regulators and attorneys.

Existing regulators are constrained by national and industry boundaries, Large warned. "This hardly mirrors the working of today's global financial businesses and markets which they must supervise, nor the inherent systemic dangers of our time," he said.
Contrasting banking and securities regulation in the United States and Britian, Large attributed differences to the two nation's different experiences during the Great Depression in the 1930s.

In the United States, the depression caused widespread bank failures and a stock market crash, leading to the creation of the Securities and Exchange Commission and separation of banking from other financial sectors, Large noted.
In Britian, regulators did not overhaul their regulations until much later in the Financial Services Act of 1986, he said.
This has possibly caused some overregulation of sophisticated investors in the United States and underregulation of market abuses affecting retail customers in Britian, he said.
"We could see already that some activity bypassed the USA, just because regulations intended for one purpose inadvertently bit in other areas," Large said.

In Britian, by contrast, "we have not been good at fighting market abuse," Large said. "There is much that the UK could profitably learn from the way in which you deal with people who abuse regulated markets and the advantages of having a civil option operating in parallel with the criminal."

In many areas, regulatory schemes between the two countries will converge, Large predicted. U.S. regulators will focus more on the needs of sophisticated investors while in Britian, regulators will "learn from your experience of how to handle market abuse."
Large declined to comment on the SIB's ongoing investigation of the Sumitomo Corp copper market scandal. "In due course all will be revealed," he said in response to a question from the audience.
Speaking to reporters after the speech, Large again declined to comment. "There are too many imponderables," he said. The investigation will wrap up "as soon as possible. The matter is continuing."
